title: Anti-vaccine sentiment is not new: Jenner's own book is full of people cursing him
dek: This episode shows the anti-vaccine movement is as old as vaccines themselves; phage SPO1 uses liquid-liquid phase-separated condensates to switch transcriptional phases; ancient smallpox DNA from South America confirms transmission by European colonization; and declining reading plus AI-generated content threaten our powers of discernment.
why: It covers phage phase-separation mechanisms, the evolutionary history of variola virus, the historical thread of anti-vaccine argument, and the fight over vaccine policy. Dense with information, and worth the time.
who: Researchers, medical students and science-minded listeners who follow virology, phage regulatory mechanisms, vaccine policy and evolutionary biology.
skip: The listener-tools segment from 1:49 to 1:52 can be skipped, but the discussion of declining reading after 1:52 is worth hearing.

points.h: A vaccine is not a bottle of soda; it is half a milliliter
points.body: The United States has signed an executive order that attempts to reduce the number of childhood vaccines and to split up the MMR vaccine. The hosts call this ‘absurd’ and cite a commentary by Jake Scott at CIDRAP, which notes that Trump claimed children are injected with a volume of vaccine equivalent to a bottle of soda, when a vaccine is typically only half a milliliter — a difference of more than 200-fold from a 20-ounce soda. The piece also rebuts claims such as vaccines causing autism.

points.h: Experts were replaced by ideological loyalists, and a court ruled it illegal
points.body: Rich fills in the background: after taking office, RFK fired the sitting Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), a body made up of experts whose recommendations are the basis on which states distribute vaccines. RFK installed non-expert ideological loyalists in their place, and the vaccine schedule they proposed was ruled illegal by a court. The new executive order is another attempt; it is expected to be challenged as well, but it will create confusion among parents and damage trust in the medical system.

points.h: The phage has to act early, because once σA binds it cannot be evicted
points.body: GP27 is the key protein that forms the condensate: its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) binds DNA, while its folded region interacts with the beta subunit of RNA polymerase. GP33 is an inhibitor of the host sigma factor σA; it binds between σA and the beta subunit and blocks the transcription complex from entering a productive transcription state. Competition experiments show that if σA binds first, GP33 cannot displace it — which is why the phage must suppress host σA early.

points.h: Smallpox was carried into the Americas by European colonization: the first molecular evidence
points.body: A new paper reports the earliest ancient smallpox genomes from South America, recovered from two individuals from the Inca colonial period in northern Chile, dated to roughly 1492-1631. The phylogeny places them within a European medieval lineage, providing the first molecular evidence that smallpox entered the Americas through European colonization.

points.h: Smallpox gene loss is a continuing process that had already begun in medieval times
points.body: In the CAM208 genome, 49 genes are deleted or inactivated. Of these, 37 are inactivated in both the ancient and modern genomes, 2 are unique to the CAM lineage, and 10 are inactivated in CAM and in modern smallpox but variable in the medieval genomes. This supports the view that gene inactivation is an ongoing process, and that some genes had already begun to be inactivated in the early medieval period.

points.h: The marginal notes in Jenner's own book are today's anti-vaccine talking points
points.body: Rich shares a scan he found of an original copy of Jenner's An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, and discovered that the book once belonged to the Southampton Anti-Vaccination League: its pages carry a large number of handwritten annotations by anti-vaccinationists. For example, where Jenner says cowpox virus can render a person permanently immune to smallpox, the annotation reads ‘nonsense’; where Jenner notes that blacksmiths are often resistant to smallpox inoculation, the annotator attributes it instead to their being physically fit from their labor. These notes are indistinguishable from contemporary anti-vaccine rhetoric.

points.h: Reading is not an instinct, and AI makes judgment scarcer still
points.body: Brianne shares The Atlantic's article ‘The End of Reading’, which notes that in 2022 fewer than half of adults had read any book at all. The article argues that reading is not a human instinct — it has to borrow other regions of the brain — and that television and the internet have crowded out the time for it. On AI, the article argues that AI-generated prose is fluent but lacks originality, and may erode people's powers of discernment and judgment, which are precisely the capacities that will be needed more in the future.

points.h: The man talking nonsense is also holding the nuclear launch codes
points.body: Charles recommends a piece by Derek Lowe, which quotes the U.S. president on vaccines: ‘I've seen where they have a vaccine thing that looks like a bottle of soda in size, and they pour it into a little kid.’ Derek calls this ‘gibberish’, and points out that this man is not only fantasizing his way to health policy but also controls the nuclear launch codes.
